Daraxonrasib works around that problem by binding RAS to a chaperone protein, letting it block the mutated signal regardless of which of the seven known RAS mutations is driving a given patient's tumor, a broader reach than earlier RAS-targeted drugs built for just one mutation.

In a Phase 3 trial of 500 patients with previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer, those taking daraxonrasib lived a median of 13.2 months, compared with 6.6 months for those on standard chemotherapy, roughly doubling survival time. Some patients on the drug lived for years, an outcome rare enough for this disease that oncologists in the room when the data was first presented reportedly gave it a standing ovation. The drug comes as two pills a day, sparing patients the infusions and harsher side effects that come with chemotherapy.

Doctors are already looking past this one approval. Because the same RAS mutations that drive pancreatic cancer also turn up in a significant share of lung and colorectal cancers, researchers see daraxonrasib and the wave of pan-RAS inhibitors behind it as a template that could extend well beyond the disease it was approved for first. One oncologist involved in the trial described envisioning a future where chemotherapy is no longer needed for pancreatic cancer patients at all.

For a cancer that has seen disappointingly little progress in survival rates over the past few decades, doubling the time patients have, and doing it with a pill instead of an IV, counts as a genuine turning point rather than an incremental gain.

stories.headline: Retired Logger Revives a Drowning Baby Otter With Mouth-to-Mouth
stories.summary: In Alert Bay, British Columbia, Gordon Mellish freed three baby otters tangled in a fishing net, and when one wasn't breathing, revived it with mouth-to-mouth resuscitation. After a week of rehabilitation the otter was released back to its mother and siblings.
stories.narrative:
Gordon Mellish, a retired logger in Alert Bay, British Columbia, was going about his day this month when he came across three baby otters caught in a fishing net. He worked to free them one by one, but the third pup wasn't moving and wasn't breathing by the time he got it loose. Rather than assume it was too late, Mellish did the only thing he could think of: he gave the otter mouth-to-mouth resuscitation.

It worked. The otter began breathing again, and a local resident named Robin Quirk stepped in to look after the recovering animal overnight, keeping it in her car and singing it a lullaby before arranging its transport to a wildlife rescue center the next day. Over the following week, staff at the center nursed the pup back to full health.

Once it had recovered, the otter was released back into the water where it was found, and reunited with its mother and siblings, who were still in the area. In an unexpected coda to the story, the otter is reported to now recognize Quirk when she whistles the same lullaby tune she sang to it during that first anxious night, swimming closer whenever she does.

Mellish, asked about wading into a stranger's emergency without hesitation, put it simply: a life's a life, no matter what it is, and you try your best to save it. It's a modest way of describing an act that took a retired logger's quick thinking, a neighbor's overnight care, and a wildlife center's expertise to turn what looked like a lost cause into a family of otters made whole again.

stories.headline: Pakistan Creates a 250-Mile Protected Corridor for the World's Second-Rarest River Dolphin
stories.summary: Pakistan's Punjab government established the new Punjnad Indus River Dolphin Sanctuary and linked it with an existing reserve in Sindh, creating roughly 250 miles of continuous protected habitat for the endangered Indus River dolphin. The corridor adds 123 miles of newly protected river to safeguard one of the world's rarest freshwater mammals.
stories.narrative:
The Indus River dolphin is one of the rarest mammals in the world, a nearly blind freshwater cetacean that navigates its murky home entirely by echolocation. Decades of dam-building and irrigation projects sliced its historic range into isolated fragments, and today only around 2,000 of the dolphins remain, split across separated stretches of the Indus in Pakistan, making it the second-rarest river dolphin species on the planet.

This week Pakistan's Punjab government took a significant step toward reversing that fragmentation, formally establishing the Punjnad Indus River Dolphin Sanctuary and linking it to an already-protected stretch of river in neighboring Sindh province. Together, the two protected areas now form a roughly 250-mile corridor of legally safeguarded habitat, including about 123 miles of river that had no formal protection before. An estimated 440 dolphins live in the Punjab stretch of the new sanctuary alone.

The push follows decades of work by conservation groups including WWF, which has been involved in Indus dolphin conservation since the 1990s, tracking population trends and pressing for exactly this kind of connected protection. Dolphins are apex predators in their river ecosystem, and safeguarding them tends to safeguard everything beneath them in the food chain too, from fish stocks to water quality, making the sanctuary as much about the health of the wider river as about the dolphins themselves.

Connectivity matters for a species like this in a way it might not for animals that can travel over land. A dolphin trapped in one isolated pocket of river, cut off by dams and barrages from populations elsewhere, faces a shrinking gene pool and no way to reach new habitat if its own stretch degrades. A continuous, protected corridor gives the population room to move, mix and rebuild in a way that scattered, disconnected reserves never could.

It's a rare piece of good news for a species that spent the last half-century mostly losing ground, and a sign that the population's decline, if not yet reversed, has at least found firmer footing.

stories.headline: Alison dos Santos Breaks the 400m Hurdles World Record
stories.summary: Brazil's Alison dos Santos ran 45.80 seconds in the 400m hurdles at the Diamond League meet in Zurich, breaking Karsten Warholm's five-year-old world record and becoming just the second man ever under 46 seconds. The run capped a comeback from a serious knee injury that once threatened his career.
stories.narrative:
At the Weltklasse meet in Zurich, Brazil's Alison dos Santos ran the 400m hurdles in 45.80 seconds, breaking the world record of 45.94 that Karsten Warholm had held since his legendary run at the Tokyo Olympics five years earlier. Warholm, running in the same race, finished second in 46.69 and watched someone else's name go into the record books instead of his own.

The rivalry between the two has defined the event for years. Dos Santos beat both Warholm and American Rai Benjamin at the 2022 World Championships, in a race many consider the deepest 400m hurdles field ever assembled, and looked to be entering the prime of his career. Then, in early 2023, he tore the meniscus in his right knee doing something as ordinary as a plank exercise, and needed surgery that sidelined him for months. He fought his way back to a World Championship final that same year, but his times sat well below his best as he rebuilt.

By 2024 his form had returned to something close to pre-injury levels, and in Zurich it went further than that, past anything he, or anyone besides Warholm, had ever run. Dos Santos becomes only the second man in history to break 46 seconds in the event, a barrier that stood as one of track and field's most exclusive clubs.

Warholm, for his part, was gracious in defeat, if visibly stung by it. He admitted the record had bothered him for years to hold and to lose, and said he would need to go back to the drawing board to find something new. The two had raced each other closely just four days earlier in Poland, close enough that Warholm said he hadn't seen this coming.

For dos Santos, the record closes the loop on a comeback that was never guaranteed. A career-threatening injury at what should have been his peak could easily have ended his run at the top of the sport. Instead, three years later, he owns the fastest 400m hurdles time in history, a testament to what a long, uncertain recovery can still lead to when it works out.

stories.headline: Retirement Home Residents' 'Kindness Kruise' Surprises a Small Town's First Responders
stories.summary: For "Be Kind to Humankind Week," residents of the Dirigo Pines retirement community in Orono, Maine, loaded gift bags and handwritten letters onto their community bus and delivered them to the town's police and fire departments, thanking the first responders who regularly support them.
stories.narrative:
Every year, the town of Orono, Maine, sends staff out to help residents of the Dirigo Pines retirement community with things like voter registration and other everyday errands that get harder to manage later in life. This year, during "Be Kind to Humankind Week," the residents decided to return the favor.

They loaded their community bus, nicknamed for the occasion the "Kindness Kruise," with gift bags full of mugs, candy and cookies, along with handwritten letters, and rode it over to the Orono Public Safety Facility to surprise the town's police officers and firefighters in person.

The gesture landed exactly as intended. Firefighter and EMT Alex Mooney said he'd taken the job just to help people, not looking for anything in return, but that having someone go out of their way to show they cared meant a lot, and made him feel warm inside. It's a small-scale story, a busload of retirees and some homemade treats, but it's also a tidy example of a town's care for its people running in both directions rather than just one.

stories.headline: India's Asiatic Lion Population Grows 70% Over the Past Decade
stories.summary: India's latest official count found 891 Asiatic lions in Gujarat's Greater Gir Landscape, up 70% from 523 a decade ago, with the lions' range expanding by roughly 15% as well. The species once dwindled to as few as 60-80 individuals in the 1980s and exists nowhere else in the wild.
stories.narrative:
The Asiatic lion is one of conservation's genuine turnaround stories, and the latest numbers out of India make the case for that better than most. According to the 16th official population estimation, conducted in May 2025 and presented by India's Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav around World Lion Day, the Greater Gir Landscape in Gujarat is now home to 891 lions, up 70 percent from 523 just a decade ago, and up 32 percent in the last six years alone.

That is a remarkable recovery for a subspecies that exists nowhere else in the wild. By the 1980s, hunting and habitat loss had pushed the Asiatic lion down to somewhere between 60 and 80 individuals, all confined to the Gir Forest. Conservationists have spent the decades since rebuilding not just the lion population itself but the ecosystem underneath it, restocking the nilgai, sambar, spotted deer and wild pig populations that lions depend on for food.

The lions haven't just multiplied, they've spread. Their range now covers close to 35,000 square kilometers across 11 districts, up from about 30,000 in 2020, and lions have begun recolonizing areas on their own that they had been absent from for generations. The Barda Wildlife Sanctuary, once empty of lions, now supports 17 that live there year-round, repopulated not through relocation programs but through the animals finding their own way back.

Because every wild Asiatic lion on Earth descends from that same small, cornered population, having them concentrated in one landscape has always carried real risk, since a single disease outbreak or environmental disaster could threaten the entire subspecies at once. The gradual spread into new territory, driven by the lions themselves rather than engineered by conservationists, is part of what makes this recovery feel durable rather than fragile: a population that is no longer just surviving in the place it was cornered, but expanding back into the range it once had.

stories.headline: Scientists Double the Nursery Population of One of Australia's Rarest Orchids
stories.summary: After three years of lab work to crack the specific fungal partnership the rosella spider orchid needs to germinate, Australian scientists and volunteers transplanted more than 500 hand-reared seedlings into the soil, more than doubling the estimated wild population of one of the country's most endangered plants.
stories.narrative:
The rosella spider orchid is about as rare as flowering plants get. It survives in just four known locations in Australia, all packed into an area smaller than a single Melbourne suburb, and as recently as the year 2000 there were only around 120 known wild plants left. Like many orchids, it can't simply be grown from seed the way most plants can; its seeds need a specific species of fungus in the soil to trigger germination at all, a partnership that took researchers years of lab work to identify and reproduce.

Having finally cracked that fungal relationship, scientists and volunteers spent three years growing rosella spider orchid seedlings from scratch, starting them in petri dishes, moving them into flasks, and eventually transplanting them into soil, where they spent roughly another year establishing themselves before being ready for the wild. In July, that work paid off: more than 500 of the hand-reared seedlings were planted out at a privately managed site, more than doubling the number of these orchids that existed in cultivated, protected conditions.

The timing lines up with genuine progress in the wild population too. Surveys found roughly 600 wild rosella spider orchids by 2023, up fivefold from the 120 recorded in 2000, suggesting that habitat protection and careful management at the plant's few known sites had already been paying off even before this latest reintroduction effort.

The rosella spider orchid is just one of eight threatened plant species being reintroduced into the wild by Australian conservationists this year, part of a broader push to rebuild native plant populations that get far less public attention than endangered animals but are just as vulnerable to extinction. For a species that has spent most of the past few decades clinging to a handful of sites with a population barely above a hundred, having more orchids now growing in cultivation than existed in the wild at the start of this century is a genuine turnaround, achieved one painstakingly cultivated seedling at a time.

stories.headline: 82 Zebra Shark Pups Released in the First-Ever Rewilding of a Shark Species
stories.summary: A global consortium of 60 aquariums across 15 countries has released 82 captive-bred zebra shark pups into a protected sanctuary off Raja Ampat, Indonesia, the first time any shark species has been actively rewilded. Wild zebra sharks had dwindled to an estimated 20 adults in the area before the program began.
stories.narrative:
Zebra sharks once ranged widely across the reefs of the Indo-Pacific, but by 2019 a survey of Raja Ampat, one of their last strongholds off eastern Indonesia, turned up an estimated 20 adults. Fishing pressure and the trade in shark fins had done to zebra sharks what it has done to so many shark species worldwide, quietly emptying reefs of an animal most people barely notice is missing until it's gone. This month, that decline started running in reverse.

A conservation program called ReShark, working with roughly 60 aquariums across 15 countries, released 82 captive-bred zebra shark pups into a 46,000-square-kilometer marine sanctuary in Raja Ampat. It's believed to be the first time any shark species has been the subject of an active rewilding effort, rather than the more common conservation approach of setting up protected areas or managing fisheries and hoping populations recover on their own.

The process behind those 82 pups took years to build. Zebra sharks lay eggs that can be collected and hatched without removing wild animals from the ocean, so aquariums around the world, coordinated through the program's founding site at Singapore's SEA Aquarium, raised eggs and pups in captivity before transferring them to nurseries in Raja Ampat and Phuket, Thailand. Specially trained aquatic husbandry staff, informally nicknamed shark nannies, cared for the pups at each stage until they were roughly a meter long and ready for release into the wild.

Mark Erdmann, ReShark's executive director, described the project's niche within shark conservation directly: most efforts revolve around protecting habitat or managing how many sharks fishing fleets can take, but this one is about actively rebuilding a population that had already crashed. The released pups now carry satellite tags, letting researchers track their movements and survival in the years ahead.

It will be a long wait to know if it worked. Zebra sharks take five to twelve years to reach sexual maturity, so researchers don't expect to see the first evidence of these pups breeding on their own until around 2028. But the release itself, 82 individuals, three years of foundational work, and a coalition spanning three continents' worth of aquariums, is already a milestone: proof that when a species is pushed to the edge of a single reef system, humans can still choose to rebuild it one pup at a time, rather than simply document its disappearance.
